court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: The defendant leased a house for six months specifically to operate as a boarding house, relying on the landlord's representation that it was in good, tenantable order. The court held that if the landlord knowingly misrepresented the house's condition, and the tenant justifiably relied on that representation instead of inspecting himself, the tenant could abandon the premises and defeat the landlord's claim for rent; a new trial was ordered because this was a jury question, not one for the court to decide as a matter of law.

quotes.text: the defendant hired the house for the purpose of keeping a boarding-house, but from the causes above stated, it was not suitable for such a purpose, and that the defendant could not, in consequence, secure and keep as many boarders as he otherwise would have been able to have done, to his damage
There is no implied warranty on the part of a landlord that a house is fit for occupation

a material representation by him to the tenant, which he knows to be false, as to the condition of the house, and upon which representation he is advised at the time the tenant for certain reasons means to rely upon, is quite another matter

holding_summary: A tenant leased a suite of rooms in the plaintiff's apartment house, the 'Four Seasons,' for one year, then abandoned the premises after about six months, claiming the rooms were rendered untenantable by vermin (bedbugs, cockroaches, water bugs, ants). The court held the landlord owed no implied warranty of habitability absent fraud or an express condition, applying caveat emptor to the leasing of the rooms just as to a sale, and affirmed judgment for the landlord for the unpaid rent.

quotes.text: The action is on a written lease of a suit of rooms in the apartment house of the plaintiff, known as the “Four Seasons.” The hiring was for one year from November 1, 1882

The maxim caveat emptor applies to the leasing as well as to the transfer of real or personal property, and the lessee or purchaser takes the risk of its quality and condition, unless he protects himself on the subject by express agreement.
The landlord, in the absence of fraud or express condition, is not responsible for the presence of rats, mice, bugs or roaches about his premises.

notes: Treats the letting of rooms/suites in an apartment house as an ordinary lease governed by caveat emptor, with no special duties or restrictions imposed because the subject is furnished living quarters — favorable to letting as an ordinary incident of ownership. who_was_letting is coded commercial_operator because the plaintiff owned and operated the multi-unit 'Four Seasons' apartment house as a rental business, not a single householder letting part of his own home.
